356	**Naden, "Enforcing Fortress' Return Type Rule at Runtime"** (2012-08-31,
357	`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/RTRinstantionTheory.tex`, with the notes of
358	May to July 2012 beside it).
359	- *Proposed:* adding bounds from the call's static return type to run-time
360	  instantiation "without changing which function definition will be chosen"
361	  (`:73-80`).
362	- *Proved:* a theorem that under the Return Type Rule the return-type bounds
363	  are satisfiable exactly when applicability is, so they can join the

365	- *Not done:* the bound-generation algorithm and the open coding (`:84-89`).

367	**POPL 2019 against these.**
368	- It carries out the second write-up in a full calculus, with proofs: the

374	- It does not do what that write-up rejected: the static type chooses the

450	- **The `covariant` keyword (row 404, POSITIONS 2026-09-26).**
451	  - FGFV is the formal account of the 2012 `covariant` and `contravariant`
452	    modifiers: position checks, the ancestor rule relaxed by variance, and
453	    overloading rules unchanged.
454	  - It also says what carrying variance to run time takes beyond
455	    variance-aware subtyping of reified types: the static return type at
456	    every call (p. 11:7).
457	  - It is the design reference for worklist item 12 when that is taken up.
458	    It changes nothing in row 404's standing as future work off the path to
459	    microGPT.
460	  - Its variance is on type parameters only. Sign flags as covariant
461	    parameters (probe `Q3Phantom`) would be an extension.
462	- **`comprises` read on values (item 26, POSITIONS 2026-09-29).**
463	  - The paper has no closed types, so it says nothing on reading a
464	    `comprises` clause, and its "obvious" addition is not shown.
465	  - Its Meet Rule asks for a declaration whose domain is equivalent to the
466	    intersection ([Meet-Third]), and Theorem 4.1 gives a unique most specific
467	    declaration for static types and ilks alike. So it keeps static
468	    uniqueness, the property item 26 gives up for closed traits in favour of
469	    run-time uniqueness.
470	  - What it shares with item 26's rung W is the run-time shape: a statically
471	    sorted most-to-least-specific list scanned for the first fit (p. 11:17;
472	    `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`, batch 7b's line on item 26).
473	  - Its proofs are over a whole program, so the closure caveat of row 487 has
474	    no counterpart.
475	- **F-bounded functions in the library (no decision yet; for batch 8 and the
476	  switch-over).** Generic functions such as
477	  `opr BIG MIN[\T extends StandardMin[\T\]\](g: Generator[\T\]): T`
478	  (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1929`) are outside FGFV on two counts: they
479	  are top-level operators, and their type parameter appears in its own upper
480	  bound (restriction (2), p. 11:11).

   440	Collecting constraints $\C$ that make a type $\alpha$ different from

   442	subtype, non-subtype, equivalence, non-equivalence, exclusion, and
   443	non-exclusion relations.  A constraint is inductively defined with
   444	boolean literals, true and false, and simple type relations like subtype,
   445	non-subtype, exclusion, and non-exclusion relations as base cases,
   446	and conjunction and disjunction of constraints as inductive steps.
   447	We also defined the various type relations inductively on the structure
   448	of types.  In addition, we defined all the type relations in a way that
   449	supports complete and disjoint case analysis for types.  The entire type
   450	relations are formally defined in Appendix~\ref{app:condrel}.
   451	
   452	%Lastly, the subtype relation of arrow types is used only in \rncite{Return-Test}
   453	Arrow types are compared only in rule \rncite{Return-Test},
   454	to see whether the return type of a more specific
   455	generic method declaration can be a subtype of the return type of a less
   456	specific one.  As the informal rule in Section~\ref{sec:motiv:fgf}
   457	specifies, Return Type Rule checks that for two declarations
   458	$d_1$ and $d_2$ where $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$, and
   459	for any non-$\Bottom$ type $\gamma$ that $d_1$ is applicable to,
   460	the return type of an instance of $d_2$ that is applicable to
   461	$\gamma$ is a supertype of the return type of some instance of
   462	$d_1$ that is applicable to $\gamma$.
   463	When the arrow types of $d_1$ and $d_2$ are
   464	$\foralltypeb{\kappa}{\arrowtype{\alpha}{\rho}}$ and
   465	$\foralltypeb{\kappa'}{\arrowtype{\alpha'}{\rho'}}$, respectively,
   466	\rncite{Return-Test} checks this by checking whether the arrow type of
   467	$d_1$ is a subtype of
   468	$\foralltype{\bar{\kappa},\bar{\kappa'}}{\arrowtype{\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}}{\rho'}}$.
   469	Since $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$ and is applicable to $\gamma$,
   470	there exist substitutions $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ that make $d_1$ and
   471	$d_2$ applicable to $\gamma$, respectively, thus both $\sigma_1\alpha$
   472	and $\sigma_2\alpha'$ are supertypes of $\gamma$, therefore so is
   473	$(\sigma_1\compose\sigma_2)\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}$.
   474	Thus, if the arrow type of $d_1$ is a subtype of
   475	$\foralltype{\bar{\kappa},\bar{\kappa'}}{\arrowtype{\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}}{\rho'}}$
   476	using some substitution $\sigma$, it makes $\sigma\alpha$ a supertype of
   477	$\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}$, which makes
   478	$(\sigma_1\compose\sigma_2\compose\sigma)\alpha$ a supertype of $\gamma$,
   479	and $\sigma\rho$ a subtype of $\rho'$.

   481	one that makes the instance of $d_1$ that is applicable to $\gamma$
   482	and has the return type that is a subtype of the instance of $d_2$.

   484	for any instance of $d_2$ instantiated with $\sigma_2$
   485	that is applicable to $\gamma$, there exists an instance of $d_1$
   486	instantiated with $\sigma_1\compose\sigma_2\compose\sigma$
   487	that is applicable to $\gamma$ and has a return type that is a subtype

   492	existential types, we extend the subtype relation of

   510	For any method invocation, there always exists a unique most specific
   511	method declaration in its set of applicable method declarations.

   515	\begin{tabular}{l@{~}l}

1	\section{Motivation}\label{sec:motiv}
     2	In this section, we first discuss existing research achievements in
     3	the pursuit of formally defining object-oriented languages with symmetric
     4	multiple dispatch, multiple inheritance, and parametric polymorphism with
     5	variance.  Then, we present how FGFV completes the long-standing endeavor
     6	by defining a core calculus with static overloading rules and a dynamic
     7	dispatch algorithm that are proven type-sound.
     8	
     9	\subsection{Overloading Rules for Multiple Inheritance}\label{sec:motiv:ff}
    10	As we discussed in Section~\ref{sec:intro}, both symmetric multiple
    11	dispatch and multiple inheritance may cause ambiguous method calls
    12	that cannot be resolved at run time.  Let us assume that class $C$ is the only
    13	subtype of both classes $A$ and $B$, and they are all distinct
    14	throughout this section.  Consider
    15	the following overloaded method declarations of $m_1$:
    16	\[\begin{array}[ht]{l@{\hskip2em}l}
    17	\hbox to 12 em{$m_1(x \COLON B, y \COLON C) \COLON B = \cdots$\hfil} & 
    18	\hbox to 12 em{$m_1(x \COLON C, y \COLON B) \COLON B = \cdots$\hfil}
    19	\end{array}\]
    20	which have the same return type $B$ but different domain types
    21	$\tuple{B,C}$ and $\tuple{C,B}$.  For a method invocation $m_1(c, c)$
    22	where the run-time type of $c$ is $C$, it is ambiguous which declaration
    23	to invoke due to symmetric multiple dispatch: both method declarations
    24	are applicable to $(c, c)$ since both $\tuple{B,C}$ and $\tuple{C,B}$ are
    25	supertypes of $\tuple{C,C}$, and neither declaration is more specific
    26	than the other.  Also, consider the following overloaded declarations of
    27	$m_2$:
    28	\[\begin{array}[ht]{l@{\hskip2em}l}
    29	\hbox to 12 em{$m_2(x \COLON A) \COLON \TYP{Boolean} = \cdots$\hfil} &
    30	\hbox to 12 em{$m_2(x \COLON B) \COLON \TYP{Boolean} = \cdots$\hfil}
    31	\end{array}\]
    32	which have domain types $A$ and $B$, respectively.  For a method invocation $m_2(c)$,
    33	it is ambiguous which declaration to invoke due to multiple inheritance:
    34	both declarations are applicable to $c$ and neither declaration is more
    35	specific than the other.
    36	
    37	In order to guarantee that no such ambiguous method calls are possible
    38	at run time, researchers have proposed several calculi with restrictions
    39	on overloaded method declarations.  CF~\cite{ff}, Core Fortress, is a core
    40	calculus of the Fortress programming language~\cite{fortress}, which contains
    41	components, top-level functions, functional methods, and declarations
    42	of exclusive types in addition to multiple inheritance.  However, it
    43	does not specify the language semantics and informally provides rules
    44	for valid overloaded method declarations.  FFMM~\cite{ffcoq},
    45	Featherweight Fortress with Multiple Dispatch and Multiple Inheritance,
    46	simplified CF to focus only on multiple inheritance, and it has a
    47	complete formalization of the language semantics including overloading
    48	rules and its type soundness proof in Coq.  Since the overloading rules
    49	of CF and FFMM are the same, we will refer to these two languages collectively as
    50	\textit{Featherweight Fortress (FF)}.
    51	
    52	The overloading rules of FF require every pair in a set of overloaded
    53	method declarations to satisfy \emph{one} of the following rules:
    54	\begin{description}
    55	\item[\textbf{Exclusion Rule:}] Their domain types are \textit{exclusive}
    56	(their intersection is $\Bottom$, where the $\Bottom$ type is a subtype of every type and
    57	no value belongs to $\Bottom$).
    58	
    59	\item[\textbf{Subtype Rule:}] The domain type of one declaration is
    60	a strict subtype of the domain type of the other, and the return type of
    61	the former is a subtype of the return type of the latter.
    62	
    63	\item[\textbf{Meet Rule:}] The domain types are not exclusive nor in a
    64	subtype relation, and the overloaded set contains a third disambiguating
    65	method declaration which we call the \textit{meet} of the pair.
    66	The meet of two method declarations is more specific than each of the
    67	declarations and less specific than any other method declaration that is
    68	more specific than both declarations.
    69	\end{description}
    70	
    71	Let us revisit the previous examples, with an additional
    72	method declaration each for $m_1$ and $m_2$:
    73	\[
    74	\begin{array}[ht]{@{}l@{$\;$}l@{$\;$}l@{\hskip2.5em}l@{$\;$}l@{$\;$}l@{\hskip2.5em}l@{$\;$}l@{$\;$}l}
    75	d_1^1:\ m_1(x \COLON B, y \COLON C) \COLON B &=& \cdots 
    76	& d_1^2:\ m_1(x \COLON C, y \COLON B) \COLON C &=& \cdots 
    77	& d_1^3:\ m_1(x \COLON C, y \COLON C) \COLON C &=& \cdots \\
    78	d_2^1:\ m_2(x \COLON A) \COLON \TYP{Boolean} &=& \cdots
    79	& d_2^2:\ m_2(x \COLON B) \COLON \TYP{Boolean} &=& \cdots
    80	& d_2^3:\ m_2(x \COLON C) \COLON \TYP{Boolean} &=& \cdots
    81	\end{array}\]
    82	Note that, for both $m_1$ and $m_2$, the third method declaration is the
    83	meet of the first two declarations.
    84	% Each set of overloaded method
    85	% declarations is valid since every pair satisfies one of the overloading
    86	% rules.  For both $m_1$ and $m_2$, the pair of the first two declarations
    87	% satisfies Meet Rule, and the other pairs satisfy Subtype Rule.
    88	Each set of overloaded method
    89	declarations is valid since every pair satisfies one of the overloading
    90	rules (for $i = 1$ and $2$, $d_i^1$ and $d_i^2$ satisfy the Meet Rule; $d_i^1$ and $d_i^3$ satisfy the Return Type Rule, as do $d_i^2$ and $d_i^3$).
    91	
    92	The overloading rules guarantee two important properties: (1) no ambiguous
    93	method calls can occur at run time, and (2) types are preserved even when a
    94	method call is dispatched to a different method declaration at run time
    95	from a method declaration chosen at compile time.  In FF, Exclusion Rule
    96	is for the trivial cases where no ambiguous calls can occur, Meet Rule
    97	%plays an important role for ensuring the existence of a disambiguating method declaration,
    98	ensures the existence of disambiguating method declarations,
    99	and Subtype Rule serves a key role for type
   100	preservation.
   101	
   102	
   103	\subsection{Overloading Rules for Multiple Inheritance and Generics}
   104	\label{sec:motiv:fgf}
   105	Similarly for multiple inheritance, generics may cause ambiguous method
   106	calls that cannot be resolved at run time.  Consider the following
   107	overloaded declarations of $\mbox{\textit{sort}}$:
   108	\[\begin{array}[ht]{l}
   109	\mbox{\textit{sort}}\ob{P \extends A}(x \COLON \kwd{List^I}\ob{P}) \COLON \kwd{SortedList^I}\ob{P}=\cdots\\
   110	\mbox{\textit{sort}}\ob{P \extends B}(x \COLON \kwd{List^I}\ob{P}) \COLON \kwd{SortedList^I}\ob{P}=\cdots\\
   111	\end{array}\]
   112	Their domain types are respectively
   113	``$\kwd{List^I}\ob{P}$ where $P$ is a subtype of $A$''
   114	and ``$\kwd{List^I}\ob{P}$ where $P$ is a subtype of $B$'';
   115	for a method invocation $\mbox{\textit{sort}}(l)$ where the run-time type
   116	of $l$ is $\kwd{List^I}\ob{C}$, both declarations are applicable to $l$ and neither
   117	declaration is more specific than the other.
   118	
   119	In order to support generics as well for symmetric multiple dispatch,
   120	\citet{oopsla11} proposed new overloading rules for given generic
   121	declarations of types and methods.  Even though they did not
   122	present a specific language with generics, we refer to the underlying
   123	language as \textit{FGF}, Featherweight Generic Fortress.
   124	To support generics, the authors
   125	re-defined the terms \emph{applicability} and \emph{specificity} for
   126	generic method declarations and their overloading rules.  A generic
   127	method declaration $d$ is applicable to a type $\alpha$ if there exists
   128	an instance $D$ of $d$ that is applicable to $\alpha$, that is, the
   129	domain type of $D$ is a supertype of $\alpha$.  For example, consider
   130	the following generic method declaration:
   131	\begin{center}
   132	$m\ob{P \extends A}(x \COLON P) \COLON P = \cdots$
   133	\end{center}
   134	which has one type parameter $P$ with an upper bound $A$.  It is
   135	applicable to $\Bottom$, $C$, and $A$, because they are subtypes of $A$.
   136	% In addition,
   137	In general,
   138	a generic method declaration $d_1$ is more specific than
   139	$d_2$ if the applicable set of $d_1$ is a subset of that of $d_2$, where
   140	the \textit{applicable set} of a method declaration is a set of types

1	<!-- The recheck of `judgement.md` (2026-09-29, `9172ab41f`) against the full text of Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance", PACMPL 3 (POPL 2019), article 11, 28 pages, read whole from `research/decks/popl19w.txt` (pdftotext of `research/decks/popl19w.pdf`; both gitignored, neither committed). Asked by Pavol through the coordinator the same day: "what if it contains important information that we should do something differently?" When the judgement was written the record had the paper only secondhand (`explorations/reviews/mie-probes/literature.md` § 1). Reading and judgement only; nothing measured. Page numbers are the paper's (11:1 to 11:28); line numbers are the text file's. Written on the branch `wip/decisions-review-popl` from `origin/main` at `5c7f115ea`, `main` being closed while batch 6.5b lands. -->
     2	
     3	# The POPL 2019 paper against the judgement: what changes
     4	
     5	## In short
     6	
     7	- The paper confirms the large calls: the exclusion rule kept, the tower flat, the 2009 overload sentence gone, the three rules, the return-type rule in the form batch 7b's rung C plans, applicability and specificity on declared quantified domains, and the implicit bound `Any`.
     8	- It contradicts one default and one mechanism, both in batches not yet run or cheap to change: item 30's "least instance" is the 2012 rule the paper says the team could not prove and abandoned; the checker's binding of an unconstrained type parameter to `Bottom` (rows 447, 425, 516) is what the paper's model forbids outright. The paper's rule for both is the same sentence: instantiate at the intersection of the upper bounds, the declared bound and the call's static return type, never at the value's type alone and never at `Bottom`.
     9	- It adds four things the record lacked: that rule; the exact form of the overloading rules with "existential reduction"; a restriction that its proof needs (a method type parameter may not appear in another's upper bound), which the library's `SUM`, `BIG MAX` and `Integral` families break; and a phase-5 requirement, that the dispatcher must know the call's static return type at run time.
    10	- Three things should be done differently, all cheap: item 30's sentence in 7b's rung S and one test pair in rung C; the `Bottom` binding replaced by the bound in one checker rung, which replaces the "treat as a throw" fix the judgement recommended for row 447; row 516's union replaced by the bound. Nothing on route A, answer 9, item 26 or the conversion order changes.
    11	
    12	## 0. What the record knew, and what the paper says
    13	
    14	The record's account (`literature.md` § 1) was right as far as it went: the paper keeps the invariant-instantiation exclusion through its ancestor rule, moves the return-type check to run time, and has no self types and no numeric tower. What it did not have, each checked in the text:
    15	
    16	- The instance rule. "The Fortress team had assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the type to be used for that type parameter. We considered this and the hybrid technique ... but we were unable to complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques. Since the minimum requirement for a type to instantiate a method type parameter is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the type parameter, the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of the upper bounds." (§ 5.4, p. 11:25, lines 1274-1284.) The rule itself is [Solve-Step] (§ 5.2.3, p. 11:19, lines 965-1016): the substitution for a parameter is the intersection of its computed upper bound and its declared upper bounds, checked against the lower bounds; "Because g' is a ground type, the solving step never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom."
    17	- The static return type at run time. Dispatch "seeks the most specific method declaration with a dispatchable instance that is applicable to the ilk of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the annotated static return type" ([R-Method], § 5.2.1, p. 11:17, lines 888-896); "the language semantics needs to make the static types of method invocations available at run time" (§ 2.3, p. 11:7, lines 329-331). The upper bound of a return-only parameter comes from that static return type ([Dispatch], line 875: `g match ρ - bounds`).
    18	- The default bound. "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (§ 3.2, p. 11:9, lines 418-419). `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface syntax" (line 438).
    19	- The overloading rules in checkable form (§ 4, Figure 5, p. 11:13, lines 630-661): No Duplicates as non-subtyping of domains either way; Meet as exclusion, subtyping or a third declaration whose domain is equivalent to the intersection ([Meet-Third], line 645); Return Type as one universal subtyping check, `arrow(d1) ⊑ ∀[κ,κ']((α ⊓ α') → ρ')` ([Return-Test], lines 656-660). Specificity is subtyping of existentially quantified domains, "a sound approximation of the subset relation of applicable sets, [but] not complete" (§ 4.2, p. 11:13, lines 673-675), narrowed by "existential reduction", which collects the constraints that keep a domain off `Bottom` and solves them (lines 733-743, Figure 6).
    20	- A restriction the proof needs. A method's type parameter bindings are well formed only if "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" and every reference falls within a left-to-right scope; "restriction (1) makes dynamic dispatch more efficient and restriction (2) makes it consistent" (§ 3.3, p. 11:11, lines 565-570); the one-pass right-to-left solve depends on it (lines 1010-1016, 1258-1262). Trait type parameters carry no such restriction.
    21	- What the calculus leaves out. "FGFV omits functional methods [Allen et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious way" (§ 1, p. 11:3, lines 142-144); "FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types in their work, [but] they can be added in an obvious way" (§ 6, p. 11:25, lines 1302-1303). No coercion, no `nat` parameters, no numbers.
    22	- The exclusion rule's form and date. [Anc-Same-Trait] (Figure 4, p. 11:11, lines 530-532): a class extending two instances of a trait must extend an instance below both; "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' ... was introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase" (§ 5.4, p. 11:24, lines 1230-1232). His homepage (© 2011, https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~kbn/) says "I am a third year PhD student in the Computer Science Department at Carnegie Mellon University" and "I spent the summer of 2011 as an intern at Oracle Labs East working on the Fortress programming language." Current affiliation: not established. A public org chart lists a "Karl Naden" as Principal Consultant at J2 Interactive (https://theorg.com/org/j2-interactive/org-chart/karl-naden), but no page found names both him and CMU or Fortress, and LinkedIn refused the fetch.
    14	- Other type-group work: Kim and Ryu, CPP 2011 (a Coq model without generics, per POPL 2019 p. 11:4), and Kim, Ryu, Luchangco, Steele, APLAS 2013, doi:10.1007/978-3-319-03542-0_11 (abstract not reachable: the publisher elides it at Semantic Scholar and Springer redirects to login). The Semantic Scholar citation list of the OOPSLA 2011 paper (https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:10.1145/2048066.2048140/citations) has 19 entries. Beyond these three it shows no later paper by Kilpatrick, Hilburn, Allen or Luchangco on the subject.
    15	- **No published resolution of the tower conflict and no proof that the rule is necessary were found.** The published results prove soundness with the rule, and the only necessity argument remains Naden's `BadList` counterexample.
    16	
    17	## 2. Julia
    18	
    19	- Single abstract inheritance, concrete leaves. "concrete types may not subtype each other: all concrete types are final and may only have abstract types as their supertypes … It turns out that being able to inherit behavior is much more important than being able to inherit structure, and inheriting both causes significant difficulties in traditional object-oriented languages" (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/types/, introduction). The tower is `abstract type Real <: Number`, `Integer <: Real`, `Signed <: Integer` and `primitive type Int32 <: Signed 32 end`, `Int64 <: Signed 64` (same page, "Abstract Types", "Primitive Types"). `Int32` is not below `Int64`. Parameters are invariant: "even though Float64 <: Real we DO NOT have Point{Float64} <: Point{Real}".
    20	- The formal account calls it "nominal single subtyping" and says: "There is no notion of soundness in Julia, even for fully type-annotated programs. If a method call does not have a most specific method, a runtime error will be reported. Ambiguity in dispatch is always resolved dynamically." (Zappa Nardelli et al., *Julia subtyping: a rational reconstruction*, OOPSLA 2018, doi:10.1145/3276483, pp. 113:3-4, https://hal.science/hal-01882137/document). The manual's example `g(x::Float64, y)` beside `g(x, y::Float64)` gives "MethodError: g(::Float64, ::Float64) is ambiguous", with the advice "specifying an appropriate method for the intersection case" (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/methods/, "Method Ambiguities").
    21	- Follows from those two facts (not stated in a source): each type has one declared supertype and invariant parameters, so a value reaches each parametric ancestor through one chain, and `where T` binds from it. Naden's `BadList` cannot be declared, specialised methods beside generic ones are allowed, and no static return type is promised to break.
    22	- Why no multiple inheritance. Bezanson's thesis (*Abstraction in Technical Computing*, MIT 2015, https://worrydream.com/refs/Bezanson_2015_-_Abstraction_in_Technical_Computing.pdf) lists "Intersections, multiple inheritance" among features that "would be difficult to add, or possibly break decidability of subtyping" (p. 63). Under "Simulating multiple inheritance" it presents Tim Holy's trait-by-dispatch pattern, noting "The original author of a type like Array does not need to know about this property, unlike the situation with multiple inheritance or explicit interfaces" (p. 74, citing github.com/JuliaLang/julia/issues/2345#issuecomment-54537633). The manual documents it as "Trait-based dispatch" ("Holy-trait" pattern, methods manual).
    23	- Julia issue #5, "abstract multiple inheritance" (Karpinski, 2011-04-27, still open, https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/issues/5), proposed allowing it under one restriction: "If two abstract types are are [sic] used for dispatch in the same 'slot' of the same generic function object then they cannot share a common, concrete descendant". That is an exclusion requirement in the spirit of Fortress's meet rule. It never shipped.
    24	- Mixed arithmetic goes through promotion, not subtyping. `+(x::Number, y::Number) = +(promote(x,y)...)` and "the arguments of functions are never automatically converted"; also "although every Int32 value can also be represented as a Float64 value, Int32 is not a subtype of Float64" (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/conversion-and-promotion/; thesis pp. 90-91). On Fortress specifically: its "coerce feature … a built-in notion of type widening … It is not possible to provide these features in Julia without doing violence to our 'everything is a method call' semantics" (thesis p. 94).
    25	
    26	## 3. X10
    27	
    28	- X10 follows Java's rule: "Limitation: A class or struct may not implement two different instantiations of a generic interface. In particular, a class or struct can implement only one function type." (*X10 Language Specification* v2.6.2, §4.6 Function types, p. 48, Wayback copy of x10.sourceforge.net/documentation/languagespec/x10-262.pdf; the same sentence is in v2.1 of 2011-02-23, p. 50, https://www.classes.cs.uchicago.edu/archive/2011/winter/32102-1/reading/x10-latest.pdf). No reason is given.
    29	- Numbers are structs, which "do not have superclasses, and cannot extend anything" (§4.2.2, p. 33). Mixing goes through implicit widening: "Byte < Short < Int < Long < Float < Double" (§11.23.2, p. 178). Overloads are chosen statically: "Method resolution is the problem of determining, statically, which method … should be invoked" (§8.12, p. 133).
    30	- Its generics are reified (*Fast method dispatch and effective use of primitives for reified generics in managed X10*, X10 Workshop 2012, doi:10.1145/2246056.2246060). The Java back end loses that for one self-typed interface: mapping "x10.lang.Comparable[T] … to java.lang.Comparable … results in the lost of runtime type information for Comparable[T]" (§18.2, p. 244).
    31	
    32	## 4. The multiple-dispatch line
    33	
    34	- None of the pre-Fortress systems had type parameters. The OOPSLA 2011 paper says of Dubious, MultiJava and F(EML): "None of the systems described above support polymorphic functions or types" (`Papers/Types/related-work.tick:36`). POPL 2019 repeats this (p. 11:25) and adds that ML≤ "lacks multiple inheritance" and that ParaSail "does not support covariant and contravariant type parameters".
    35	- Cecil combined multimethods, multiple inheritance and F-bounded generics by erasing type arguments from dispatch: "Method lookup does not depend on the instantiating types … message sends foo[int]() and foo[string]() will always be dispatched to the same method implementation" (*The Cecil Language: Specification and Rationale*, §4.1.2, http://projectsweb.cs.washington.edu/research/projects/cecil/www/Vortex-Three-One/doc-cecil-lang/cecil-spec-82.html). Its tower puts the self-typed trait at the root only: `extend num isa ordered[num]`, then "num can have subtypes, such as int or float, which can be compared with each other … extend int isa num; extend float isa num; 3 != 3.14 -- legal" (§4.4, …/cecil-spec-86.html). Litvinov's 2003 thesis (ftp.cs.washington.edu) timed out.
    36	- Tate, Leung, Lerner (*Taming Wildcards in Java's Type System*, PLDI 2011, https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~ross/publications/tamewild/tamewild-tate-pldi11.pdf), the source Naden cites for the unique minimal instantiation: "For Java this invocation is always unique, although this is not necessary for our algorithm" (§4.2, p. 5).
    37	- Later work POPL 2019 cites: FHJ (Wang et al. 2018), whose dispatch "uses static types at run time", and Castagna et al. 2015, "a statically-typed calculus with dynamic (explicit) dispatch through pattern-matching" (p. 11:26). No other paper on soundness with multiple dispatch, reified generics and multiple inheritance together was found.
    38	
    39	## 5. Other languages with generics and one generic interface twice
    40	
    41	- **Java** forbids it: "different parameterizations of the same generic interface … This requirement was introduced in order to support translation by type erasure" (JLS SE 21 §8.1.5, https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-8.html). The reason is erasure, not dispatch. The OOPSLA paper's "it is already required in Java" (`exclusion.tick:154-156`) borrows the rule without that reason.
    42	- **C#** (reified) allows it except where two instantiations "may unify for some type parameter substitutions" (CS0695, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/misc/cs0695). Overloads are resolved statically: "Overload resolution is a binding-time mechanism" (§12.6.4.1), and "Static binding takes place at compile-time", except for `dynamic` (§12.3.2) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions).
    43	- **F#** 5 added it: "You can now implement the same interface at different generic instantiations" (RFC FS-1031, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fsharp/whats-new/fsharp-50).
    44	- **Swift** has no generic protocols, and the Generics Manifesto files them under "Unlikely": "Implicit in this feature is the ability for a given type to conform to the protocol in two different ways" (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/main/docs/GenericsManifesto.md, "Generic protocols").
    45	- **Rust** allows `impl From<u8> for u64` beside `impl From<u16> for u64` (https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u64.html) and forbids only overlap: "Two trait implementations overlap when … the implementations can be instantiated with the same type" (Reference, "Trait implementation coherence", https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/implementations.html).
    46	- **Kotlin** forbids it: the supertype closure must be "consistent, i.e., does not contain two parameterized types with different type arguments" (https://kotlinlang.org/spec/type-system.html, "Simple classifier types").
    47	- **Scala** refuses it with "illegal inheritance; … inherits different type instances of trait" (compiler message, https://www.scala-lang.org/old/node/3423). No sentence found in SLS 2.13 ch. 5.
    48	- **Haskell** allows one instance per class and type: "A type may not be declared as an instance of a particular class more than once in the program" (Haskell 2010 §4.3.2, https://www.haskell.org/onlinereport/haskell2010/haskellch4.html). Instances are resolved statically.
    49	- **C++** templates instantiate distinct classes, and overload resolution selects from "a list of expressions that are to be the arguments of the call" (https://eel.is/c++draft/over.match.general). Nothing selects by instantiation at run time.
    50	- **Ceylon** (reified, multiple interface inheritance, declaration-site variance; "Like C#, and unlike Java, Ceylon's type system is fully reified") keeps the exclusion for invariant parameters and relaxes the variant ones: "for every invariant type parameter T of Y, the type argument A … given in V and … B … given in W must be exactly the same type, and, furthermore, X is a subtype of an instantiation U of Y such that U is a subtype of V&W" (spec §3.7.2 "Principal instantiation inheritance", mirror http://lucaswerkmeister.github.io/ceylon-spec/html_single/). It has no overloading at all: "Overloading is illegal in Ceylon" (§3.2.1).
    51	
    52	## 6. The self-typed algebra tower
    53	
    54	- Greenman, Muehlboeck, Tate (*Getting F-Bounded Polymorphism into Shape*, PLDI 2014, doi:10.1145/2594291.2594308, https://users.cs.utah.edu/~blg/publications/fbound/effing-bound-polymorphism.pdf) identify the pattern. Self-typed traits are "shapes", and "The primary one is to encode a form of self types … useful for binary methods … as well as algebraic operations, such as addition" (p. 3). Their numeric example: with Integer only `Summable<Integer>` and Float only `Summable<Float>`, "the join of Integer and Float does not exist"; under Material-Shape Separation "Summable is only permitted in inheritance and type-variable constraints, not as the type of an expression" (p. 7). A survey of 13.5 million lines of Java found no overlap (abstract), and the Ceylon team found one counterexample and planned adoption (p. 5). The paper does not treat dispatch. It names "type families" (family polymorphism) as the second use of shapes, not the tower.
    55	- The flat encodings in current use:
    56	  - C#: `public interface INumber<TSelf> … where TSelf : INumber<TSelf>`, implemented separately by `Int32` and `Int64` (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.numerics.inumber-1).
    57	  - Swift: generic heterogeneous operators `static func < <Other : BinaryInteger>(lhs: Self, rhs: Other) -> Bool`. The proposal "DOES NOT solve the integer promotion problem" (SE-0104, https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0104-improved-integers.md).
    58	  - Scala: type-class values `trait Numeric[T] extends Ordering[T]` and `implicit object IntIsIntegral` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scala/scala/2.13.x/src/library/scala/math/Numeric.scala, l. 221, l. 67).
    59	  - Cecil: the algebra on the root `num` only (§4).
    60	- Typed Racket nests the tower statically ("Integer is a subtype of Rational, which is a subtype of Real") with union types and "overloading with intersection types". It names the tower as the hard case for typed languages: "No existing typed language provides as rich a numeric hierarchy nor as many generic operations as those found in Smalltalk, Scheme, or Racket" (St-Amour et al., *Typing the Numeric Tower*, PADL 2012, pp. 1-2, 5, https://www2.ccs.neu.edu/racket/pubs/padl12-stff.pdf). It has no self-typed traits and no run-time dispatch on type arguments.
    61	- Apart from Naden's write-up and the 2012 patents, no source was found that treats a nested tower carrying self-typed traits at each level together with run-time dispatch over reified generics.
    62	
    63	## What the field settled and what it did not
    64	
    65	- **Keep the rule and flatten the tower.**
    66	  - Java, Kotlin, Scala and X10 keep the rule, with flat numeric types and widening. Java's stated reason is erasure.
    67	  - The Fortress group kept the rule after 2012 (Welterweight 2012, POPL 2019), for "unique minimal instance" dispatch.
    68	  - Cecil's root-only `ordered[num]` and C#'s `INumber<TSelf>` on sibling structs are two flat shapes in use.
    69	- **Drop the rule and instantiate at the call site with no specialised overloads.**
    70	  - C#, F#, Rust and Haskell allow multiple instantiation, and every one chooses instances and overloads statically. None has run-time dispatch over generic overloads, the one place Naden's hole opens.
    71	  - Ceylon allows variant multiple instantiation and has no overloading.
    72	- **Neither route.**
    73	  - Julia avoids the trade by single inheritance and gives up static soundness ("no notion of soundness"). It keeps specialised methods and moves ambiguity to a run-time error.
    74	  - POPL 2019 keeps both the rule and specialisation by checking the static return type at run time, the option Naden rejected.
    75	  - The 2012 patents' "Self-types meet … must form a forest" admits the tower's chain of self-typed instantiations inside the rule, close to the review's route C. It was never published, and its test (`comprises T`) is absent from the library's `Equality`.
    76	- **Not settled.** Nobody published a resolution of the tower conflict under run-time dispatch, or a proof that the rule is necessary; the published proofs show only that it suffices.

    96	
    97	Figure~\ref{fig:grammar} shows the syntax of the FGFV calculus.
    98	Metavariables $T$ and $U$ range over trait names;
    99	$O$ ranges over object names;
   100	$x$ ranges over variable and field names;
   101	$z$ is either $x$ or the keyword $\KWD{self}$;
   102	$m$ ranges over method names;
   103	$P$, $Q$, $S$ range over type parameter names;
   104	and $\tau$, $\omega$, $\zeta$, $\xi$ range over types.
   105	
   106	A program consists of a sequence of class declarations and
   107	a top-level expression.
   108	A class is either a trait or an object;
   109	traits are like Java interfaces that do not have any fields, and
   110	objects are like Java final classes that cannot be extended.
   111	A trait may have type parameters with variance annotations and
   112	upper bounds, extend any number of other traits, and have method definitions.
   113	An object is similar to a trait except that (1)~its type parameters do
   114	not have variance annotations because they are always invariant, and
   115	(2)~it may have fields, which are initialized when an object instance is
   116	created.  When a class does not extend any trait, we omit the
   117	empty extends clause $\extends \bigbd{}$.
   118	When a class has no type parameters, we omit the
   119	empty brackets; we write $T$ for $T\ob{}$.
   120	A method may have type parameters as well, but they have both
   121	lower and upper bounds.
   122	We omit clauses when no bounds are specified; for example,
   123	we write $T\ob{\bindco \; P}$ for $T\ob{\bindco \; \bindup{P}{}}$ and
   124	$m\ob{Q,\bd{Q} \extends S}$ for $m\ob{\lobindup{}{Q}{}, \lobindup{Q}{S}{}}$.
   125	By default, each type parameter has an upper bound $\Any$ and a
   126	lower bound $\Bottom$, which we describe in the next subsection.
   127	
   128	The bounds of a type parameter place restrictions on valid instantiations
   129	of the type parameter; a valid type instantiation must be a subtype of
   130	all its upper bounds and, at the same time, a supertype of
   131	all its lower bounds, if any.
   132	We write $\bindco$ for covariance, $\bindcontra$ for
   133	contravariance, and $\bindinv$ for invariance.  As discussed in
   134	Section~\ref{sec:motiv:fgfv}, variance annotations of type parameters define
   135	subtype relations between different instances of a generic trait.
   136	For example, consider the following trait declarations:\\[-.5em]
   137	\[
   138	\begin{array}{l}
   139	\kwd{trait} \; U_1 \; \dontcares \; \kwd{end}\\
   140	\kwd{trait} \; U_2 \extends \bigbd{U_1} \; \dontcares \; \kwd{end}\\
   141	\kwd{trait} \; T \bigob{\bindco \; P, \bindcontra \; Q, \bindinv \; S} \;
   142	\dontcares \; \kwd{end}
   143	\end{array}
   144	\]
   145	where ``$\dontcares$'' denotes omitted material.
   146	Because $U_2$ is a subtype of $U_1$,
   147	the variance annotations of the type parameters of $T$ define
   148	subtype relations such as $T\ob{U_2, U_1, U_1} \subtypeof T\ob{U_1, U_2, U_1}$.

   224	Expressions and types are conventional.
   225	One can refer to a field or bound variable simply by mentioning it;
   226	the keyword $\KWD{self}$ refers to the target object for the currently executing method.
   227	Functions are first-class values; $((\bar{x\COLON\tau})\COLON\tau \Rightarrow e)$
   228	is a (typed) function constructor,
   229	and we write $e\apply(\bar{e})$ for
   230	function calls.  An object creation $O\obb{\tau}(\bar{e})$ makes an
   231	instance of $O$ by instantiating its type parameters with $\bar{\tau}$ and
   232	initializing its fields with the values of $\bar{e}$.
   233	While tuples are not first-class values in FGFV (they would be trivial to add,
   234	but are not needed for our purposes), we use tuple types $(\rep{\tau})$
   235	to denote the domain types of functions and methods, which may have multiple parameters.
   236	The type $\Any$ is a supertype of every type (and $\Bottom$, used below, is a subtype of every type but is intentionally not expressible in the surface syntax).
   237	
   238	
   239	\subsection{Well-formedness}\label{sec:wellformed}
   240	
   241	We define well-formedness of a program and its declarations as shown in
   242	Figure~\ref{fig:wellformed}.
   243	A type-declaration environment $\Delta$ is a set of class declarations and
   244	type parameter bindings, and
   245	a variable-type environment $\Gamma$ is a sequence of bindable variables
   246	and their types.  Checking well-formedness may introduce
   247	\textit{internal types}:
   248	\begin{center}
   249	$\descsm{Internal type} \quad \alpha~::= P~\mid~C~\mid~\tupleb{\alpha}~\mid~
   250	\arrowtype{\alpha}{\alpha}~\mid~\Any~\mid~\Bottom~\mid~
   251	\uniontype{\alpha}{\alpha}~\mid~\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha}$
   252	\end{center}
   253	which contain $\Bottom$, union types, and intersection types.
   254	Type $\Bottom$ is a subtype of every type; hence, $\Any$ and $\Bottom$
   255	are the top and bottom, respectively, of the type lattice.
   256	Metavariables $\alpha, \gamma, \rho, \chi, \eta$ range over internal types.
   257	We introduce metavariables $K$, $C$, $J$, and $M$,
   258	analogous to $\kappa$, $c$, $t$, and $\mu$, respectively, where 
   259	types $\tau$ in the latter are replaced by internal types $\alpha$ in the former.
   260	
   261	Rule \rncite{T-Program} states that a program is well-formed
   262	if its class declarations have distinct names and are well-formed, and
   263	its top-level expression is well-formed.
   264	%%% The following material has been obsoleted by new section on notation.
   265	% We write $\emptyseq$ for an empty sequence.
   266	% Following a suggestion of Steele~\citeyearpar[0:59:37]{NEW-OLD-LANGUAGE},
   267	% we use
   268	% an underline below submaterial within overlined material to prevent the 
   269	% overline from attaching subscripts to the metavariables in the submaterial;
   270	% hence, $\rep{\jwfdecl[\same{\Delta}]{\psi}}$ represents the sequence
   271	% $\Delta\vdash\psi_1\, \mathsf{ok}\ \ \Delta\vdash\psi_2\, \mathsf{ok}\ \cdots\ \Delta\vdash\psi_n\, \mathsf{ok}$
   272	% for any appropriate $n \geq 0$.
   273	The type of a program is the type of its top-level expression;
   274	the metavariable $g$ and $h$ represents a \textit{ground type},
   275	which is a type that contains no type parameters.
   276	We describe well-formedness and type checking of expressions
   277	in Section~\ref{sec:static}.
   278	
   279	Rules \rncite{D-Trait} and \rncite{D-Object} check well-formedness
   280	of class declarations.  For the declaration of a class $C$,
   281	they verify that the type parameter names of the declaration are distinct,
   282	that the types used in the declaration are well-formed,
   283	and that the declared methods are well-formed.
   284	In addition, as we explain later in this subsection,
   285	they make sure that (1)~the \textit{proper ancestors} of $C$,
   286	which are all the traits $C$ extends, by explicitly extending and
   287	transitively inheriting as well, are well-formed, and
   288	(2)~the \textit{visible methods} of $C$,
   289	which are the methods either declared by $C$ or inherited
   290	from the traits $C$ extends, obey the overloading rules.
   291	The only differences are that rule \rncite{D-Trait} additionally
   292	guarantees that a trait does not extend itself, and rule \rncite{D-Object}
   293	guarantees that the names of the fields are distinct.
   294	
   295	Well-formedness of types is conventional
   296	as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:wellformedtypes}.
   297	The types $\Any$ and $\Bottom$ are trivially well-formed.
   298	A type parameter $P$ is well-formed under a type-declaration environment
   299	$\Delta$, if $\Delta$ contains a binding of $P$.
   300	A constructed type $T\obb{\alpha}$ or $O\obb{\alpha}$ is well-formed, if
   301	the trait $T$ or the object $O$ is declared in the given
   302	type-declaration environment and all the type arguments $\rep{\alpha}$
   303	are well-formed and satisfy the declared
   304	bounds of their corresponding type parameters.
   305	Finally, the remaining structural types such as tuple types, arrow types, 
   306	union types, and intersection types are well-formed,
   307	if all their component types are.

    95	\section{Overloading Resolution}\label{sec:resolve}
    96	Method overloading is resolved both at compile time for type checking
    97	and at run time for evaluation, and these
    98	\textit{static and dynamic overloading resolutions} should be consistent.
    99	For a method invocation expression, static overloading resolution
   100	chooses an instance of the most specific method declaration that is
   101	applicable to the static types of the method arguments;
   102	dynamic overloading resolution then must select an instance of the
   103	most specific method declaration that is applicable to the dynamic types
   104	of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the static type of
   105	the expression.
   106	% In this section, we describe the static and dynamic
   107	% overloading resolutions in detail, prove that they make type-sound
   108	% selections, and discuss the design decisions for FGFV.
   109	
   110	\subsection{Static Overloading Resolution}\label{sec:static}
   111	As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:motiv:fgfv}, in order to make
   112	type-sound choices, the static types of
   113	method invocation expressions must be available at run time.
   114	Thus, checking well-formedness of an expression $e$ produces its
   115	type-annotated version $\epsilon$ and its type $\alpha$
   116	as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:wellformedexpr}.  A \textit{type-annotated
   117	internal expression} is just like an expression except that all the
   118	method invocation expressions in it are annotated with their static
   119	types:
   120	\begin{center}
   121	$\descsm{Type-annotated internal expression} \quad
   122	\epsilon~::=~z~\mid~((\bar{x\COLON \alpha})\COLON \alpha \Rightarrow \epsilon) ~\mid~\epsilon\apply(\bar{\epsilon})~\mid~O\obb{\alpha}(\bar{\epsilon})~\mid~\epsilon.m(\bar{\epsilon})\COLON \alpha$
   123	\end{center}
   124	
   125	We focus on rule \rncite{T-Method} for method invocation, since
   126	the rules for the other kinds of expressions are conventional.
   127	For a method invocation $e.m(\bar{e'})$,
   128	after checking well-formedness of expressions $e$ and $\bar{e'}$,
   129	the rule performs static overloading resolution via rule \rncite{MSAV}
   130	to find an instance of the most specific applicable visible method declaration,
   131	and annotates the method invocation with the return type of
   132	the chosen instance.  Rule \rncite{MSAV} first selects the most
   133	specific applicable visible method declaration $d'$ with a set of
   134	substitutions $\setb{\sigma'}$ using the static types of the method
   135	arguments $\alpha$.
   136	The unique existence of the most specific applicable visible 
   137	method declaration is guaranteed by Theorem~\ref{thm:mostspecific}.
   138	Then, the rule selects one instance $D$ out of instantiations of $d'$
   139	with $\setb{\sigma'}$.

   151	target languages and their type systems, they all define a set of
   152	\emph{overloading rules} that overloaded method declarations should
   153	satisfy to make dynamic dispatch select the most specific applicable

   156	For a simple object-oriented language with multiple inheritance,
   157	\citet{ff, fortress} and \citet{ffcoq} presented three overloading rules:
   158	Exclusion Rule, Subtype Rule, and Meet Rule.

   199	In this paper, we
   200	present a formal core calculus \emph{FGFV} (Featherweight Generic Fortress with Variance)

Thus, overloaded definitions whose domain types exclude each other
trivially satisfy the Meet Rule: 
there are no types (other than \Bottom) 
to which both definitions are applicable.
Exclusion allows us to describe explicitly what is 
typically implicit in single-inheritance class hierarchies.

In our previous work on Fortress without generics~\cite{allen07}, 
we provided a special rule---the \emph{Exclusion Rule}---%
to exploit this information.
However, 
the Exclusion Rule can also be viewed, 
as we do in this paper, 
as a special case of the Meet Rule, 
where there are no nontrivial types 
to which both definitions are applicable.

Fortress provides three mechanisms to explicitly declare exclusion \cite{Fortress}:
an `object` declaration, a `comprises` clause and an `excludes` clause.
We describe these precisely in Section~\ref{sec:exc-spec}, 
but for now, we simply note that 
they do not help with the overloaded `tail` function.
Specifically,
even with these exclusion mechanisms, 
we cannot define `List` 
so that the definitions for `tail` satisfy the Return Type Rule.

To see this, 
consider the following overloaded definitions (from Section~\ref{sec:intro}):

\small
`  tail[\T\](x: List[\T\]): List[\T\]
  tail(x: List[\ZZ\]): List[\ZZ\]
`
\normalsize
and the following type constructor declaration:

\small
`  BadList <: { List[\ZZ\], List[\String\] }
`
\normalsize
Both definitions of `tail` are applicable to the type `BadList`,
and the monomorphic one is more specific.
Two instances of the generic definition are applicable to this type:

\small
`  tail(List[\ZZ\]): List[\ZZ\]
  tail(List[\String\]): List[\String\]
`
\normalsize
The Return Type Rule requires that 
the return type of each of these instances 
be a supertype of the return type of the monomorphic definition
(the monomorphic definition is its only one instance); 
that is, it requires 
`List[\ZZ\] <: List[\ZZ\]` 
and `List[\ZZ\] <: List[\String\]`.
The latter is clearly false.

\chapter{Overloading and Multiple Dispatch}
\chaplabel{multiple-dispatch}

\note{Keyword and varargs parameters are not yet supported.}

Fortress allows functions and methods (collectively called \emph{functionals})
to be \emph{overloaded}.  That is,
there may be multiple declarations for the same functional name
visible in a single scope (which may include inherited method declarations),
and several of them may be applicable to any particular functional call.

However, with these benefits comes the potential for ambiguous calls at run time.
For an overloaded functional call,
the most specific applicable declaration is chosen, if any.
Otherwise, any of the applicable declarations such that
no other applicable declaration is more specific than them is chosen.


In this chapter, we describe how to determine which declarations
are \emph{applicable} to a particular functional call,
and when several are applicable, how to select among them.
We also provide overloading rules for the declarations of functionals
to eliminate \emph{some possibility} of ambiguous calls at run time,
whether or not these calls actually appear in the program.
\secref{overloading-terms} introduces some terminology and notation.
In \secref{functional-applicability},
we show how to determine which declarations
are applicable to a \emph{named functional call}
(a function call described in \secref{function-calls}
or a naked method invocation described in \secref{naked-method-calls})
when all declarations have only ordinary parameters
(without varargs or keyword
parameters).
We discuss how to handle dotted method calls
(described in \secref{dotted-method-calls})
in \secref{dotted-method-applicability},
and declarations with varargs and keyword
parameters in \secref{applicability-with-special-params}.
Determining which declaration is applied,
if several are applicable,
is discussed in \secref{resolving-overloading}.


\section{Principles of Overloading}
\seclabel{overloading-terms}

Fortress allows multiple functional declarations of the same name to
be declared in a single scope.  However, recall from \chapref{names}
the following shadowing rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
dotted method declarations shadow top-level function declarations with
the same name, and
\item
dotted method declarations provided by a trait or object declaration
or object expression
shadow functional method declarations with the same name that are
provided by a different trait or object declaration
or object expression.
\end{itemize}
Also, note that a trait or object declaration
or object expression must not have a
functional method declaration and a dotted method declaration with the
same name, either directly or by inheritance.
Therefore, top-level functions can overload
with other top-level functions and functional methods,
dotted methods with other dotted methods,
and functional methods with other functional methods and top-level functions.
It is a static error if any top-level function declaration is
more specific than any functional method declaration.
If a top-level function declaration is overloaded with a functional method
declaration, the top-level function declaration must not be more specific than
the functional method declaration.


Operator declarations with the same name but different fixity
are not a valid overloading; they are unambiguous declarations.
An operator method declaration whose name is one of the operator parameters
(described in \secref{opr-ident})
of its enclosing trait or object may be overloaded with other operator
declarations in the same component.
Therefore, such an operator method declaration
must satisfy the overloading rules
(described in \chapref{overloaded-declarations})
with every operator declaration in the same component.

\note{This restriction will be relaxed.}

Declarations with the same functional name may have different static
parameters, or some of them may have static parameters and others none.
A declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose
parameter type ranges over every instance of it whose static arguments
satisfy their bounds: it is applicable to a call when some such instance is
(\secref{functional-applicability}), and it is compared with other
declarations on the parameter types they declare, taken over all their
instances (\secref{resolving-overloading}).
A declaration without static parameters is the case with none.
The rules that a set of such declarations must satisfy are given in
\chapref{overloaded-declarations}.

\chapter{Overloaded Functional Declarations}
\chaplabel{overloaded-declarations}

\note{Return types are required for overloaded functional declarations.}

Fortress allows multiple functional declarations to be in scope of a
particular program point.  We call this overloading.
\chapref{multiple-dispatch} describes
how to determine which overloaded declarations are
applicable to a particular functional call, and when several
are applicable, how to select the most specific one among them.
In this chapter, we give a
set of rules on overloaded declarations that guarantee there
exists a most specific declaration for any given functional call.
These rules are complicated by the presence of coercion, which may
enlarge the set of declarations that are applicable to a functional
call, as discussed in \chapref{conversions-coercions}.



\section{Principles of Overloading}
\seclabel{principles-overloading}

Fortress allows multiple functional declarations of the same name to
be declared in a single scope.  However, recall from \chapref{names}
the following shadowing rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
dotted method declarations shadow top-level function declarations with
the same name, and
\item
dotted method declarations provided by a trait or object declaration
or object expression
shadow functional method declarations with the same name that are
provided by a different trait or object declaration
or object expression.
\end{itemize}
Also, note that a trait or object declaration
or object expression must not have a
functional method declaration and a dotted method declaration with the
same name, either directly or by inheritance.
Therefore, top-level functions can overload
with other top-level functions and functional methods, dotted methods with
other dotted methods, and functional methods with other functional methods
and top-level functions.

Overloading functional declarations allows the benefits of polymorphic

\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that a single

applicable, and that the one the dynamic call runs is more specific than it.
With the closed-trait case of the Meet Rule, a static call whose argument's

34:## What walk checks
35-
36-Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
37-
38-Under walk, the disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses a program's own top-level type that has the name of a type of `FortressLibrary`, such as `Index` or `Indexed`: "Type name may refer to: Index, FortressLibrary.Index". Give such a type another name.
39-
40-At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. It makes no stand-in, and so checks nothing through one, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where its static parameters, `where` clause or `extends` clause raise an error at the symbolic types. It refuses:
41-
42-- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and messages for the pairs below. The team's check looks for a position where the two parameter types neither nest nor exclude. If a parameter type there mentions a static parameter, the message is "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". If neither does, it is "are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present". The pairs:
43-  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
44-  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length, only where one of them has a varargs parameter. Walk checks no other pair of lists of different lengths;
45-  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations, nor a generic one beside a plain one, nor a generic function beside a generic trait's or object's functional method that has no static parameters of its own;
46-  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.
47-
48-  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
49-  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
50-  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
51-  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
52-  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
53-  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
54-  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
55-  - It does not refuse a type that extends a self-typed trait `T[\A\]` and is not an `A` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). A call that both `T`'s operator and another declaration fit then runs one of them, without an ambiguity error (ledger row 893). Make each type that extends `T[\A\]` an `A`.
56-  - It loads a generic top-level function whose declared domain lies inside that of a self-typed trait's functional method of the same name, where the Return Type Rule holds. The checker refuses every top-level function more specific than a functional method of its name, a check that the specification does not state: '… is more specific than the declaration of the functional method' (ledger row 894).
57-  - It loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 806).
58-  - It loads a type that provides two functional symbolic operators, such as two `||`, that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 611).
59-
60-  The paths differ on `f[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: T)` beside `f(x: Z)`, where `K comprises { A, B, C }`, `Z excludes { A, B }`, and `C` is an object that extends `Z` but not `R`. Walk refuses the pair: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker reads the bounds, finds that no value lies in both domains, and accepts it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 713).
61-- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods in a type that provides both, where their name is an identifier or an operator named by a word, as `MAX`.
62-- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
63-- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. Where a listed type names a bounded type `where`-clause variable, as `NBox[\E\]` in `comprises { NBox[\E\] } where [\E extends Number\]`, walk ignores the variable's bound, and runs `NBox[\String\]` (ledger row 754). # Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild

**tree**
: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.

**library order**
: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.

**DSL grammar**
: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.

**parser directory**
: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.

## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:

- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.

## Two layers of code

The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.

The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.

The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:

- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.

An edit makes stale what was built from it:

- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.

## The caches

All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:

- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).

Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).

## The library order

The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.

Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:

- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.

content.content:
# Writing a test

**gated test**
: Test that the gate's suites run.

**green**
: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as passed.

**red**
: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as failed.

**`XXX` test**
: Gated expected failure. It asserts the answer that the specification gives, and fails today. The harness reports it green while it fails, and red when the defect is fixed.

## A test program

A test program has this form:

    component Name
    export Executable

    (* declarations *)

    run(): () = do
        assert(f(2), 4, "f(2)")
    end

    end

- `(*)` starts a comment to the end of the line. It cannot hold `*)`: the parser ends the comment there and refuses the program. `(* ... *)` comments nest.
- A compiled test with a `run` key ends `run()` with `println("PASS")`, unless a `run_out` key checks its output (below).
- Under walk, `assert(x, y, msg)` checks that `x` equals `y`. It and `=/=` call a type's own `=` only if the type extends a `FortressLibrary` trait that declares `=`, such as `Equality` (ledger row 807). Otherwise they compare by `SEQV` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). If a type `P` has its own `=`, make `P` extend `Equality[\P\]`, or write `assert(x = y, msg)`. The compiler's library declares the two-value `assert` only for `ZZ32`, `String` and `Character`; its `assert(flag, msg)` takes any `Boolean`.
- Do not name a variable or a parameter after a functional method of the library, such as `big`, `even`, `numerator` or `shift`. The disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses it: "Variable even is already declared."
- Under walk, a numeral does not bind to `NN32` or `NN64`, and a numeral with a radix point does not bind to `RR32` (ledger row 454). Write `a: NN32 = unsigned(5)`, not `a: NN32 = 5`.

## Where a test goes, and how it passes

Interpreter (walk): write `ProjectFortress/tests/Name.fss`, whose component is `Name`.

- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
- the linker's aliasing of apis;
- `fortress unparse`;
- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.

If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.

## One test, or a few

Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.

### Interpreter tests

Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]

- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.

To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.

An abstract functional method also counts for it. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's `+` between an array and a number, because a type can extend both the trait and `Number`, which has no `comprises` clause (P-160).
